title: Retirement and the Last Third of Life
subtitle: A whole generation is being handed twenty or thirty years past the career and told the goal is endless leisure, a permanent vacation earned by forty years of work. Scripture has a different word for the last third of life. Not retirement from usefulness but a change of assignment. Not the idol of the endless vacation but fruitfulness in age, a finishing that is also a sowing, a legacy of faith handed forward before the hands let go.

connections.label: Work as Worship: calling does not end when the paycheck does
Aging and the Body: the last third lived in a weakening frame
Facing Death: the horizon the last third can no longer ignore
Generosity and the Open Hand: the legacy of what you release
Take stock of the whole shape of your life with the life audit

parts.title: The Real Struggle
parts.body:
The party is over and the quiet is louder than you expected. They gave you a card and a cake and a clock, and Monday morning you woke up with nowhere to be and a calendar that no longer fills itself. The first few weeks felt like a long-awaited vacation. Then the vacation did not end, and somewhere in the third month you stood in the kitchen at ten in the morning and could not say what the day was for. Nobody warned you that the hardest part of retirement is the loss of being needed.

For forty years the question of what your life was about was answered for you by the work. You were the one who fixed the thing, closed the deal, ran the floor, taught the class, raised the kids who are now raised and gone. Your worth had a job description, and now the job is gone, and underneath the relief is a question you did not know was hiding there. If I am not what I did, then what am I. The culture has no answer for this. It told you the goal was to stop, and it never told you what to do with the stopping.

I have buried men three years into retirement who, by every account, died of nothing the doctors could name except the disappearance of a reason to get up. And I have sat with others, more than I can count, who reached the finish line they had aimed at for decades, the boat, the warm climate, the unbroken leisure, and found it strangely empty, a permanent Saturday that began to feel like a slow erasure. The endless vacation, it turns out, is not paradise. It is the absence of a purpose dressed up as a reward.

There is a particular ache in this season that the younger do not see coming. It is the ache of watching your relevance shrink. The phone rings less. The opinions you offer are received more gently and weighed less. The world you helped build is now run by people who do not remember you built it. And the temptation in that ache runs two directions. Either you grasp, clutching at influence and refusing to let go, becoming the elder who cannot bless the young because he is still competing with them. Or you withdraw, deciding that since you are no longer central you will be absent, and spending the richest years you have left on hobbies and screens and a slow disengagement from everything that matters.

I am not writing this from a safe distance, watching the old struggle from the vantage of the young. I am a pastor who has spent fifteen years near this passage, watching faithful people approach the last third of life with no map for it, having spent forty years preparing financially for retirement and not one hour preparing spiritually. We have planned the money and starved the meaning. And the result is a generation arriving at the most potentially fruitful season of life with no idea what it is for.

parts.title: Why It Matters
parts.body:
Because the last third of life is not a postscript. It may be a quarter or a third of your entire span, twenty or thirty years, longer than your childhood, longer than your career was at the time you started it, and the question of what those years are for is not a small one. To treat them as a long wind-down is to write off a span of life large enough to do more lasting good than all the busy decades that came before. The stakes are not whether you will be comfortable. The stakes are whether a third of your life will count.

It matters because the endless vacation is not neutral. It is an idol, and like every idol it promises rest and delivers emptiness. The culture sold you a picture of the good ending, the perpetual leisure earned by labor, and the picture is a lie not because rest is bad but because human beings were not made to be useless, and a creature made in the image of a working God cannot be happy doing nothing for thirty years. The boat does not save. The warm climate does not save. The endless Saturday becomes, for many, a slow drowning in comfort, and the saddest funerals I conduct are often for people who had everything they aimed at and arrived at the end with nothing to show for the years but the absence of trouble.

It matters because how you handle the loss of relevance reveals what your relevance was built on. If your worth was in your usefulness, then retirement is a kind of death, and you will either rage against it or sink under it. But if your worth was always in being a beloved creature of God, then the loss of your role is not the loss of your self, and you are freed to do in this season what the busy years never allowed, to be fruitful without needing to be central, to bless without needing to compete, to give yourself away without keeping score. The way you age is the final exam on what you actually believed about where your value came from.

It matters because the church needs its elders and is starving for them. We have built churches around the energy of the young and quietly retired the old to the back rows, and we are paying for it in a generation of believers with no one to show them how to finish well. The aging saint who has walked with God for fifty years, who has buried a spouse and survived a prodigal and kept the faith through a long unanswered prayer, possesses something no conference can manufacture and no young pastor can fake. To waste that on shuffleboard is a theft from the body of Christ.

And it matters because the watching world, and especially your own grandchildren, are learning from how you age what they may hope for from their own end. They are watching to see whether faith holds up when the strength goes, whether a life lived for Christ finishes well or finishes bitter, whether the gospel is good news even when the body fails and the relevance fades. Your last third is a sermon, and it may be the most important one you ever preach, because it is the one delivered when you have nothing left to gain by preaching it.

parts.title: The Biblical Vision
parts.body:
The Bible does not contain the word retirement, and the absence is not an oversight. The one place Scripture comes close, the Levites who stepped back from the heavy lifting of the tabernacle at fifty, tells the whole story. They were released from the strenuous labor and immediately reassigned, to minister to their brothers, to guard, to teach the younger. The form of the work changed. The vocation did not. That is the biblical pattern for the last third in a single image. Not retirement from usefulness, but redeployment into a different kind of fruitfulness.

Start with the picture Scripture paints of the aged righteous, and notice that it is not a picture of decline but of fruit. The Psalmist says the righteous flourish like the palm tree, and then drives the point home, they still bear fruit in old age, they are ever full of sap and green, planted in the house of the Lord. The Bible's vision of a faithful old age is not a fading but a fruiting, a tree heavy with what it has spent a lifetime growing toward. The last years are meant to be the harvest of the whole life, not its long anticlimax.

Consider the parade of the aged in Scripture who did their most consequential work after the world would have shelved them. Abraham was seventy-five when God called him and a hundred when the promise arrived. Moses began his life's work at eighty. Caleb stood at eighty-five and said, give me this mountain, asking for the hardest assignment when his peers were asking for a chair. Anna the prophetess was eighty-four, worshiping in the temple night and day, and she was given to recognize the infant Messiah when the young and the busy missed him entirely. Simeon held the Christ child and sang that he could now depart in peace, a man whose final assignment was simply to see the promise and bless it. Scripture is full of people whose usefulness to God peaked when their usefulness to the labor market ended.

Watch the structure of blessing in the Bible, and notice that it runs from the old to the young by design. The dying patriarch gathers his sons and speaks a future over them. The aged Jacob blesses Joseph's boys with crossed hands. The elder is the one who hands forward the faith, who tells the story, who lays a hand on the next generation and sends them out. Psalm 71 captures the prayer of the aging saint exactly. Even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation. The old age the Bible hopes for is not a withdrawal but a proclamation, a last great act of handing on what was received.

And Scripture is honest about the cost, which keeps the vision from being sentimental. Ecclesiastes describes the days of trouble drawing near, the keepers of the house trembling, the strong men bowed, the years in which you say you have no pleasure in them, and it does not flinch from the real losses of age. The biblical vision is not a denial of decline. It is a redemption of it. The body fails, and the fruit grows, and these are not contradictions. For Paul writes that though the outer self is wasting away, the inner self is being renewed day by day, and this is the deep logic of a Christian old age. The strength leaves and the soul ripens. The relevance fades and the fruit hangs heavier. The vacation was never the goal. The harvest was. And the harvest is gathered in precisely as the strength to chase anything else runs out, so that you finish not by grasping but by giving, not clutching the world you helped build but blessing the ones who will build the next, until you can say with the old man in the temple, now, Lord, you may let your servant depart in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation.

parts.title: The Historical and Traditional Wisdom
parts.body:
For nearly all of human history there was no such thing as retirement, and the elderly were not a problem to be managed but a resource to be honored. The aged held the memory of the tribe, the wisdom of the craft, the story of where the people came from, and a society without writing depended on them to carry forward what could be carried no other way. To grow old was to grow more valuable, not less, and the structures of village and household and church assumed the old would teach the young until they died. The very idea that a person might spend the last third of life withdrawn from all usefulness would have struck almost every previous generation as a tragedy or an impossibility.

The ancient world reflected on age with a seriousness we have lost. Cicero wrote his essay On Old Age in the year 44 before Christ, arguing against the complaint that age robs life of its pleasures by insisting that it offers higher ones, the goods of counsel and authority and reflection that the young cannot possess. The aged, he wrote, are not idle but engaged in greater and better matters, the steering of affairs by mind rather than muscle. The pagan philosopher saw what the Christian culture would deepen, that the value of a life does not run on physical strength, and that the loss of the body's vigor can be the gain of the soul's.

The monastic tradition built a place for the old that honored both their limits and their gifts. In the Rule of Benedict, written around the year 530, the elderly were released from the harshest labors and the strict letter of the schedule, treated with tenderness, and at the same time kept fully within the life of the community as those whose prayer and counsel were needed. They were not put out to pasture. They were folded into the heart of the house, their weakness accommodated and their wisdom drawn upon. The monastery had no concept of a useless member, only of members whose usefulness changed shape with the seasons of a life.

The Christian centuries developed a whole discipline of finishing well that the modern world has entirely forgotten. The medieval and Reformation church taught what they called the art of dying, a practice of preparing for the end across the final years rather than denying it until the last hour. The aging believer was meant to set his affairs in order, reconcile his quarrels, give his blessing, pass on his faith, and approach death not as a defeat to be postponed but as a passage to be made well. The Puritans wrote extensively for the old, treating the final season as a high calling with its own duties, the duty of ripening, of testimony, of leaving behind a clear deposit of faith for the children who came after.

Then modernity invented retirement, and it was at first a mercy and became a trap. The pension and the retirement age, born in the industrial era and spread across the twentieth century, rightly recognized that the body wears out and that a person should not be worked to death. But the structure that began as humane protection slowly hardened into an ideology of the endless leisure, marketed by an entire industry as the golden years, the reward of perpetual recreation, the long-deserved vacation that never ends. The factory took work from sunlight, and the pension took meaning from age, and we are now the first society in history to hand millions of healthy people two or three decades with no expected purpose and to call the emptiness a prize. The honor of the elder gave way to the management of the senior, and the wisdom of age gave way to the marketing of leisure. Nobody is going to hand the old vision back. It will have to be recovered, deliberately, by believers who decide that the last third of their life is not for sale to the leisure industry but is consecrated, like all the rest, to the God who calls until the very end.

parts.title: The Honest Engagement with Knowledge
parts.body: Christians have nothing to fear from the research on aging, purpose, and the structure of a good ending. All truth is God's truth, and the studies keep confirming what Scripture assumed, that human beings are made for purpose, that usefulness does not expire with employment, and that a life without meaning withers no matter how comfortable it is. But the research can map the territory and still misname the destination. Science can show you that purpose extends life. It cannot tell you what purpose is worth giving your last years to. So we read these honest observers with gratitude, and then we test what they say against Scripture, keeping what is true and correcting what is aimed wrong.

secular.author: Bob Buford
secular.whatItGetsRight: Buford, writing in 1994 out of his own midlife crisis, named the crucial movement that most people in the second half of life need, the shift from success to significance, from accumulating to contributing, from building a career to building a legacy. He saw clearly that the metrics that drove the first half, money, status, achievement, do not satisfy in the second, and that people who fail to make the turn arrive at the end with a full bank account and an empty life. His insistence that the later years are for giving yourself away recovers something the culture of retirement had buried.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Buford's framework is genuinely Christian in intent and still risks importing the very scorekeeping it means to escape. The danger in significance is that it can become success wearing nicer clothes, a second-half project to be achieved and measured, a legacy built to satisfy the same hungry self that built the career. Scripture roots the last third not in achieving significance but in receiving an identity already given, the beloved creature who is fruitful precisely because he has stopped needing to prove anything. The aim is not a bigger contribution but a freer one, the fruit that comes from a branch abiding in the vine rather than straining to matter.

secular.author: Atul Gawande
secular.whatItGetsRight: Gawande, in 2014, exposed with unflinching honesty how modern medicine and modern culture have failed the old and the dying, treating the end of life as a problem to be fought rather than a passage to be made well. He shows that what aging people most want is not maximal safety or maximal length but the preservation of meaning, autonomy, and connection, and that a good ending is one in which a person is still living a story they recognize as their own rather than merely being kept alive. His recovery of the questions that matter at the end cuts through decades of medical denial.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Gawande sees the failure of the deny-and-fight model and offers in its place a humane management of decline, which is wiser than what it replaces and still stops at the grave. He can help you face the end with dignity and cannot tell you the end is not the end. Scripture meets the same mortality and speaks past it, to a body that will be raised, a story that does not conclude at death but continues in the One who conquered it. The Christian wants what Gawande wants, a meaningful ending lived as one's own story, and grounds it not in the management of decline but in the hope of resurrection, which alone makes the dignity more than a brave face on an unrelieved defeat.

secular.author: Dan Buettner
secular.whatItGetsRight: Buettner's study of the world's longest-lived communities found, again and again, that the people who age best are not the ones with the most leisure but the ones with the most belonging and purpose. The elders in these places remain woven into family and community, keep working in some form, hold a clear reason to rise in the morning, and are honored rather than warehoused. The research confirms with hard data that disengagement kills and that a purposeful, connected old age is a long and healthy one. The cultures that revere their old produce old people who thrive.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Buettner documents that purpose and belonging extend life and treats long life as the prize the purpose serves. Scripture inverts the order. Purpose is not chiefly a strategy for living longer but the proper shape of a creature made in God's image, valuable even when it does not add a single year. The believer who serves and belongs in old age does so not to reach a hundred but because he was made to be fruitful, and he holds his length of days with an open hand, knowing that the goal was never the longest possible life but the most faithful possible finish, however many years it runs.

secular.author: Arthur Brooks
secular.whatItGetsRight: Brooks, in 2022, draws on research showing that the sharp analytical abilities that drive early careers decline with age, while a different kind of intelligence, the wisdom to synthesize, to teach, to see patterns and mentor others, rises in the second half. He argues that the crisis of the aging high achiever comes from clinging to the declining strength instead of stepping into the rising one, and that the path to a good later life runs through teaching, service, and the deliberate release of the things that once defined success. His distinction names exactly why so many accomplished people age badly.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Brooks maps the transition with real insight and frames it finally as a strategy for sustained personal flourishing, a way for the high achiever to keep feeling fulfilled. Scripture pushes the release further than self-fulfillment. The letting go of the first-half strengths is not merely a wiser path to continued happiness but a death, a dying to the self that was built on competence, and the fruit on the far side comes not from a clever pivot but from a cross. The believer steps from strength to strength not to preserve his sense of significance but to lose his life and find it, which is a deeper and costlier movement than career strategy can name.

secular.source: Tribe and the human need to be needed
secular.author: Sebastian Junger
secular.whatItGetsRight: Junger argues, in 2016, that modern affluence has stripped people of the thing they most deeply need, the experience of being necessary to a community, of having a role on which others depend. He observes that people are often happier in hardship that requires them than in comfort that does not, and that a society which removes the need to be needed produces a peculiar despair amid plenty. The insight bears directly on retirement, where the loss most felt is precisely the loss of being necessary, of mattering to a group that counts on you.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Junger names the hunger to be needed with great accuracy and locates its satisfaction entirely in the human tribe, which is real and not enough. The belonging he prescribes can fail, because human communities age and scatter and die, and the one who builds his whole worth on being needed by others will find, in the end, that even that is taken. Scripture answers the hunger to be needed first with the deeper truth that you are wanted, loved by God before you were ever useful to anyone, so that the believer can pour himself into being needed by his people without being destroyed when, at the very end, he is needed by no one and held only by God.

parts.title: Where Faithful People Differ
parts.body: Faithful Christians who agree that the last third is for fruitfulness rather than idleness still differ on what fruitfulness should look like, and the difference is not careless. It runs to whether the calling of the aging believer is best lived by stepping back from active labor into a settled ministry of prayer, presence, and blessing, or by pressing on in active service and refusing to slow until the body forces it. Hear each at its strongest, because both are trying to honor the same God who both calls the old to fruit and grants the weary rest, and each guards against a real danger the other can fall into.

views.view: The fruitfulness of release, stepping back into prayer, presence, and blessing
views.body: This view holds that the proper work of the last third is to relinquish the active, central roles and step into a quieter and arguably higher ministry, the ministry of the one who prays, who is present, who blesses and counsels and hands forward the faith without needing to run anything. It points to Anna in the temple, worshiping night and day, and to Simeon whose final assignment was simply to recognize and bless the Christ, and it insists that the kingdom is advanced as much by the praying elder as by the laboring young. The conviction underneath is that aging well requires a deliberate letting go, a refusal to cling to the influence and busyness of earlier years, so that the hands are free to bless rather than clenched to compete. Advocates warn that the elder who will not release his grip becomes a burden to the young, the patriarch who blocks the next generation because he cannot bear his own diminishment, and they hold up instead the dignity of the one who steps aside on purpose and finds, in the stepping aside, a freedom the busy never knew. The danger they are guarding against is real, the aging Christian whose identity is so welded to his role that he cannot let go, who clutches at relevance and sours into bitterness or control, and who never receives the peculiar fruitfulness God reserves for those willing to become small. Against that they commend the open hand, convinced that the richest harvest of a life is often gathered by the one who has finally stopped striving and learned to simply abide, pray, and bless.

views.view: The fruitfulness of perseverance, pressing on in active service to the end
views.body: This view holds that the calling to labor for the kingdom does not slacken with age and that the aging believer should press on in active, costly service until the body genuinely makes it impossible. It points to Caleb at eighty-five demanding the hardest mountain, to Moses beginning his life's work at eighty, to Paul who poured himself out to the end and refused to coast, and it insists that the temptation of age is not over-busyness but premature surrender, the comfortable disengagement that mistakes a pension for a permission to stop serving God. The conviction underneath is that the harvest needs workers, that the years of accumulated wisdom and freed-up time are a gift meant to be spent on the kingdom rather than banked, and that the believer who steps back too soon robs the church of exactly what it most needs. Advocates warn against the spiritualizing of laziness, the way a theology of release can become a pious excuse for the very leisure the gospel resists, and they hold up instead the saint who works the field until dusk and is found faithful at his post. The danger they are guarding against is real, the aging Christian who retires not only from his career but from his calling, who reads the freedom of the later years as a license to consume rather than contribute, and who arrives at the end having spent his most available decade on himself. Against that they commend perseverance, convinced that no one is ever discharged from the service of Christ, and that the crown is given to the one who finishes the race still running.

parts.title: The Formation
parts.body:
The last third of life forms you, more decisively than you might think, because it strips away the things that propped up a false self and leaves standing only what was real. The career that answered the question of your worth is gone. The strength that let you outrun your own emptiness is fading. And what is left, when the role and the vigor are subtracted, is the actual person you have been becoming all along. Aging does not change your character so much as reveal it. The last third is the season in which a life is finally seen for what it is, and that revelation is itself a kind of formation, a final shaping of the soul that no other season can accomplish.

It forms humility, if you let it, and the humility it offers is not a doctrine but a daily fact. To age is to be reminded, relentlessly, that you are not the center, that the world goes on without your contribution, that the people who once needed you have learned to manage, that your opinions are received gently and weighed lightly. This is agony to the proud and freedom to the humble. The same loss of relevance that embitters one person liberates another, and the difference is whether you ever truly believed your worth was a gift rather than an achievement. The aging believer who has made peace with his own diminishment has learned the deepest lesson there is, that he was always held by grace and never by his usefulness, and that lesson can only be fully learned when the usefulness is taken away.

It forms generosity, the open-handed letting go that the grasping years never permitted. There comes a season when a person realizes he cannot take any of it with him, that the accumulation is over and the only thing left to do with what he has gathered is to give it away, and the believer who reaches that realization early is set free to spend his last third pouring out rather than hoarding, blessing the young rather than competing with them, releasing his grip on the world he helped build. The hands that are about to let go of everything are the hands best suited to bless, and the formation of the last third is largely the loosening of the fingers, the slow glad surrender of a life that has stopped needing to keep what it cannot keep anyway.

And it forms a readiness to die, which is the strange and central work of the final season. Teach us to number our days, the Psalmist prays, that we may get a heart of wisdom, and the last third is the time when the days become impossible to ignore, when the funerals are of peers rather than elders, when the horizon that was always abstract becomes near and real. The Christian is not asked to deny this or to fight it with ever more elaborate denial. The Christian is asked to ripen, to let the nearness of the end do its proper work, to set affairs in order and quarrels to rest and blessings on the heads of the young, and to approach the passage not as a defeat but as a homecoming. The body wastes and the soul renews, the relevance fades and the fruit hangs heavier, and the person formed by a faithful last third arrives at the end able to say what the old man said in the temple, that he can now depart in peace, having seen the salvation he spent his whole life trusting. The formation, in the end, is the making of a person who can finish, who can hand it all forward and let it all go and lie down in the hope of a morning he will not have to earn.

parts.title: The Practice
parts.body: None of what follows is a retirement plan in the financial sense, and none of it is about staying busy for its own sake. It is about consecrating the last third of life to the One who calls until the end. One thing to say plainly before you begin. The losses of this season are real, and for some they are crushing. If the end of the career has tipped into a depression you cannot lift, if the loss of role has become a darkness that will not break, that is not a failure of faith to be willed away. It is a medical and pastoral matter. See a doctor. See a counselor. Talk to your pastor. Seeking help is an act of trust, not a defeat. And know that grief in this season, for the strength that is fading and the relevance that is shrinking, is honest and allowed, not a sin to be hidden. Start where you are, with one thing, and let the rest come as the season lengthens.

steps: Name out loud, to God or to a trusted friend, the actual loss underneath this season. The loss of being needed, of mattering, of the role that answered who you were. You cannot consecrate what you will not first grieve, so begin by telling the truth about what hurts.

Ask one honest question and write down the answer. If I am not what I did, then what am I. Sit with it long enough to get past the easy reply, until you reach the place where your worth either rests on grace or it does not.

Reach toward one younger person this week, not to advise but to bless. A grandchild, a young couple, a new believer. Let them know you see them and are for them. The structure of blessing in Scripture runs from the old to the young, and you are now the old.

Read Psalm 71 slowly and pray it as your own. Even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation. Let it set the prayer of your last third, that the years left would be a proclamation and not a withdrawal.

Examine the picture of retirement you absorbed without choosing it. Where did your image of the good ending come from, and is it the endless vacation the culture sold you or the fruitful harvest Scripture promises. Name the idol if it is one, and ask God for a better aim.

Take stock of what you have actually been given for this season, the freed-up time, the accumulated wisdom, the relationships, the resources, and ask not how to preserve them but how to spend them. The gifts of the last third are for sowing, not banking.

Find one place to be genuinely needed again, and let it be service rather than hobby. A ministry that requires you, a person who depends on you, a corner of the kingdom that is short of workers. The hunger to be needed is honest, and the answer is not to suppress it but to spend it on what lasts.

Begin the old practice of setting your house in order, gently and without morbidity. A quarrel to reconcile. A blessing to speak. An affair to settle. The art of finishing well is mostly the art of not leaving the important things undone, and the time to begin is before you have to.

Commit your freed time to a fruitfulness you can sustain, whether the ministry of active service or the ministry of prayer and presence, and stop apologizing for it being unpaid. The Levite who stepped back from the heavy lifting was reassigned, not retired, and so are you.

Become a deliberate mentor to someone younger, not by accident but on purpose. Take a young believer to coffee on a rhythm and let them ask you the hard questions, and hand forward what fifty years taught you. Wisdom that is not passed on dies with the one who holds it.

Reorder your giving for the season of release. As the accumulation ends, let generosity become a reflex rather than a calculation, and begin the glad letting go of what you cannot keep anyway, blessing the young and the church and the poor with the open hand of one who is going home.

Sit once this season with the reality of your own death, not in fear but in faith, and let it do its proper work. Number your days honestly. Ask what you would set right, hand forward, or stop wasting if you truly believed the horizon was near. It is.

Decide what your legacy of faith will actually be and build it on purpose. Not money. Faith. Write the story of how God kept you, record the testimony of a long obedience, leave a clear deposit of belief for the children and grandchildren who will outlive you and need to know the faith held when the body failed.

Make the last third a season of ripening rather than withering, of bearing fruit in old age as the Psalm promises, planted in the house of the Lord and full of sap and green. Stay rooted in the church, in the Word, in prayer, in the company of God's people, because the tree that flourishes in age is the one still planted by the water.

Practice the art of finishing well as a whole vocation, the deliberate work of reconciling, blessing, handing forward, and preparing for the passage. Do not drift toward the end. Approach it the way a faithful steward approaches the giving of an account, with affairs settled and quarrels healed and the blessing already spoken over the young.

Keep returning to the One the whole life was for. The career was never your worth and the leisure was never the goal. Spend your last third learning to say what Simeon said, now, Lord, you may let your servant depart in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, until the day the saying becomes your own departure, and you finish not by clutching the world you helped build but by handing it forward and lying down in the hope of a morning you will not have to earn.
